So, let the reader choose whichever interpretation he wishes, so long as he understands that such superstitious observances of times bring great peril to the soul, so much so that the apostle adds, "I am afraid, lest perhaps I should have labored in you in vain." … And yet if someone, even a catechumen, is caught observing the sabbath by the Jewish rite, the church is confused. As it is, innumerable members of the church say with great complacency in open view of us, "I do not travel on the day after the first." … Alas for human sinfulness, that we only denounce what is unfamiliar, but with familiar things we tolerate them, although they may be great and cause the kingdom of heaven to be shut against them absolutely. It is for them that the Son of God shed his blood. We come to tolerate them through frequent acquaintance with them, and through increased toleration we share in them.

"I am afraid." See, their insides are in turmoil, and Paul is afraid. The phrase "for fear that" still indicates those standing and not yet fully shipwrecked. And it gives them hope that if they are willing to recover, their labor will not be in vain for them; as he said, Remember my toil and sweat for you, and do not frustrate my anguish.

See what a sensitive heart: they waver and Paul is afraid. The expression "lest somehow" (μή πως) shows that they were still intact and had not yet suffered complete shipwreck. And he gives them hope that if they wish to come to their senses, then the labor spent on them was not in vain. He is as if saying to them: remember my efforts for you and do not make my labors futile.

By this practice they are put in grave danger. Hence he says: "I am afraid lest perhaps it was in vain," i.e., fruitlessly, "that I labored" among you. Therefore the faithful must avoid observing such things. Indeed, no suggestion of these things should be found among them, for whatever is done simply out of devotion to God can turn out prosperously.

From this arises a danger because faith in Christ profits nothing from it. Hence he says: "I am afraid of you, lest perhaps I have labored in vain among you"; and further on: "If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing" (5:2).

O trumpet of peace to the soul that is at war! O weapon that puttest to flight terrible passions! O instruction that quenches the innate fire of the soul! The Word exercises an influence which does not make poets: it does not equip philosophers nor skilled orators, but by its instruction it makes mortals immortal, mortals gods; and from the earth transports them to the realms above Olympus. Come, be taught; become as I am, for I, too, was as ye are.
Discourse to the Greeks, Chapter V

When the Apostle says to the Galatians, whom he rebukes and reproves throughout the whole epistle, Be as I am, because I am as you are (Gal. 4:12): if therefore he had made himself such as they were, it was unnecessary to say, Be as I am. Or perhaps in some things he had begun to be an imitator of them, and in others he wishes them to become like him? — What of theirs could the Apostle imitate? Or what was lacking to the teacher of the Gentiles? Rather, he exhorts them to be his imitators; and since it is not impossible, he reproves them in this way when he says, Because I am what you are: for you are human, just as I am; therefore do what I do. It can also be referred to that statement where he says that he became all things to all by agreeing with them in those points where they did not differ from the truth, especially the Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:22). For there was nothing of theirs, which ought no longer to be done, that had not previously been rightly done, such as circumcision, the observance of sabbaths, new moons, foods. But if he approved anything of the Gentiles, he did not show that it should still continue. For they say that the world was made by God and by men: this always stands. If therefore in these matters, by consenting to them, he was made as they were, he exhorts them that in a similar way they too should become as he is, agreeing with his doctrine.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 60: ON BE AS I AM (GAL. 4:12)

Be as I am, for I too am as you are. He says this so that they may take pains to correct these things; for it is not impossible that they should be as he is, since he too was what they also were, that is, a man; and when he had been in error, persecuting the Church, he was reproved and turned himself about. Brothers, I beseech you, you have done me no harm. Now he deals more gently with them and begins to recall their good things, so that after great reproofs they might be refreshed on hearing of their good works, and might take pains to reform themselves; lest, pressed too long by harsher rebukes, they become exasperated. Yet he says that they have done him no harm; for their offense was harming themselves, since the Apostle had fulfilled the office of the dispensation entrusted to him, that he should preach to them with all diligence, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: You, he says, preach: if they hear you, you will gain them; if not, you will save your own soul (Ezek. 3:21).

This is addressed to his Jewish disciples, and he brings his own example forward, to induce them thereby to abandon their old customs. Though you had none other for a pattern, he says, to look at me only would have sufficed for such a change, and for your taking courage. Therefore gaze on me; I too was once in your state of mind, especially so; I had a burning zeal for the Law; yet afterwards I feared not to abandon the Law, to withdraw from that rule of life. And this ye know full well how obstinately I clung hold of Judaism, and how with yet greater force I let it go. He does well to place this last in order: for most men, though they are given a thousand reasons, and those just ones, are more readily influenced by that which is like their own case, and more firmly hold to that which they see done by others.

Observe how he again addresses them by a title of honor, which was a reminder moreover of the doctrine of grace. Having chid them seriously, and brought things together from all quarters, and shown their violations of the Law, and hit them on many sides, he gives in and conciliates them speaking more tenderly. For as to do nothing but conciliate causes negligence, so to be constantly talked at with sharpness sours a man; so that it is proper to observe due proportion everywhere. See then how he excuses to them what he has said, and shows that it proceeded not simply because he did not like them, but from anxiety. After giving them a deep cut, he pours in this encouragement like oil; and, showing that his words were not words of hate or enmity, he reminds them of the love which they had evinced toward him, mixing his self-vindication with praises. Therefore he says, "ye did me no wrong."

Brothers, I beseech you, you have done me no injury. And you know that through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel to you some time ago.

Join what follows to the preceding sentence; and to make this clearer, let the order be the one we construct: I beseech you, brothers, be as I am, because I also am as you are. Like this is that saying: "We entreat on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20). And elsewhere too: "I beseech that first of all supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made" (1 Tim. 2:1). So also the words of Peter, who says: "The elders among you I entreat, who am myself a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ" (1 Pet. 5:1). These words indeed both summon us to humility and strike down the haughty brow of bishops who, as though set upon some lofty watchtower, scarcely deign to look at mortals and to speak to their fellow slaves. Let them learn from the Apostle that the erring and unwise Galatians are called brothers. Let them learn from him who, after rebuke, speaks gentle words: "I beseech you" (1 Cor. 11). And what he beseeches is this, that they be imitators of him, as he himself is of Christ; or rather, to keep to the present passage, what he asks is nothing great: that just as he himself for their sake was made lesser from greater, so they should climb up from lesser things to greater. In nothing, he says, have you injured me. A disciple injures his master if through his own negligence he wastes his precepts and his labor. The Galatians had not injured the Apostle, since up to the present time they were keeping his Gospel and his commandments. Or certainly thus: When I first announced the Gospel to you, and on account of the infirmity of your flesh, because you could not receive the greater mysteries, I preached to you as to little children, and pretended that I myself was weak, so that I might gain you who were weak: did you not receive me as an angel, as Christ Jesus? Since, then, you did me no injury in anything at that time, and thought me, humble and cast down for your sake, like the Son of God, how is it that, when I summon you to greater things, I am injured by you, through the waste of my labor, and that you now mourn, with the work made void, that dispensation by which I had pretended to be a little one?

Be as I also am, because I also am as you.

What he says is this: just as I became weak to you who were weak, and could not speak to you as to spiritual men but as to carnal men and little ones in Christ, and, because you were not yet able to feed on solid food, gave you only the milk of the Gospel to drink, not wishing you to remain forever in the age of infancy but to lead you little by little on to adolescence and youth, so that you might be able to take solid food: so you too ought to be as I also am, namely to have a taste for more perfect things and, leaving milk behind, to pass on to stronger foods and to greater pastures. And he says this as an imitator of the Savior, who did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave; and was found in habit as a man, so that we might become gods from men and no longer die; but, rising together with Christ, might be called his friends and brothers, and so that the disciple might be as the teacher, and the slave as the master. But it can also be understood thus: I beseech you, he says, brothers, that, despising the Jewish observance of days, months, seasons and years, which are shadows of things to come, you imitate me, who, having lived without reproach in the Law, counted all things as refuse and rubbish, that I might gain Christ. For I too was as you now are, when I was held bound by the same observances, and, because the Church of Christ did not do these things, I persecuted it and laid it waste.

"Become as I am." Yet the words are addressed to those from Judea. Become as I am. "Be imitators of me," Paul says, "for I also, having set aside the law, ran to faith." For even I, he says, was as you are, observing the law and carefully practicing it in many respects.

"for I also am as you are." I longed intensely for the law as well, but see how I have been changed. "You also," he says, "envy that change."

— [PHOTIUS] He appeals to them, considering their salvation as his own. He passes through their acts of gratitude, and the honors by which they honored him, and how greatly they regarded him, wishing to set this right, namely, that the insults now uttered against them by him were not spoken out of any dislike or hatred (for how, he says, could he have been hostile toward you, having treated you with great consideration?); but that what was said came from a mind that was anxious and loving.

To the believers from among the Jews he speaks thus: imitate me. For I too was very devoted to the law, as you are, but I left it and now contend for Christ and the faith. Be such as these yourselves. He expressed this beautifully in conclusion. For people are more readily drawn by kindred examples than by arguments.

After strong reproaches, he again displays gentleness. For harsh censure is no more beneficial than extreme leniency. Therefore he calls them brethren, reminding them at the same time of the grace of baptism, by which we all became brethren, as born of one Father – God. He also justifies the reproaches he has expressed, namely that they did not arise from hatred. For you have done me no injustice that I should become hostile toward you, but rather, you have shown me countless signs of honor and affection. How then, after this, could I be saying these things out of hatred? But I speak, without doubt, out of concern for you and out of deep gratitude toward you.

You know that through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel to you long ago: and your trial in my flesh you did not despise nor reject. He recalls to their memory the time when he first preached to them the Gospel of God. For at that very time the Apostle was beset with injuries and weakened by beatings; for he seems weak who is humbled and does not resist, for the sake of the Gospel of God. And in this he praises their constancy, that they were not drawn away from the faith: for the injuries of the Apostle were the trial of the Galatians, in which they were found firm, not doubting about the faith. For they could have taken offense and said: What power or hope is there in this faith, when its minister is so humbled? But because they had already steeped their minds in the hopes of things to come, they did not dread present perils for the name of Christ, certain that our faith has its dignity not on earth but in heaven, and that for these tribulations great rewards are repaid. He makes them blush, because after these praiseworthy things they had been circumvented, so that they appeared blameworthy.

Not to have injured one is indeed no great thing, for no man whatever would choose to hurt wantonly and without object to annoy another who had never injured him. But for you, not only have ye not injured me, but ye have shown me great and inexpressible kindness, and it is impossible that one who has been treated with such attention should speak thus from any malevolent motive. My language then cannot be caused by ill-will; it follows, that it proceeds from affection and solicitude. "Ye did me no wrong; ye know that because of an infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel unto you." What can be gentler than this holy soul, what sweeter, or more affectionate! And the words he had already used, arose not from an unreasoning anger, nor from a passionate emotion, but from much solicitude. And why do I say, ye have not injured me? Rather have ye evinced a great and sincere regard for me. For "ye know," he says, "that because of an infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel unto you; and that which was a temptation to you in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected." What does he mean? While I preached to you, I was driven about, I was scourged, I suffered a thousand deaths, yet ye thought no scorn of me; for this is meant by that which was a temptation to you in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected." Observe his spiritual skill; in the midst of his self-vindication, he again appeals to their feelings by showing what he had suffered for their sakes. This however, says he, did not at all offend you, nor did ye reject me on account of my sufferings and persecutions; or, as he now calls them, his infirmity and temptation.

But ye received me as an Angel of God. Was it not then absurd in them to receive him as an Angel of God, when he was persecuted and driven about, and then not to receive him when pressing on them what was fitting?

Now Paul announces the Gospel to the Galatians through the infirmity of the flesh, not his own but that of his hearers, who could not subject the flesh to the word of God, but, being as it were fleshly, received nothing of spiritual understanding. To make this more evident, let us set out an example. He teaches through the infirmity of the flesh who says: "If they do not contain themselves, let them marry". And: "A woman, if her husband has died, is free: let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:9, 39). But he by no means teaches through the infirmity of the flesh when he records these things: "You are loosed from a wife: do not seek a wife". And: "It is time that those who have wives be as though they had none" (ibid. 27, 29). For some precepts are given to the spiritual, others to the fleshly. And it is one thing that is commanded by way of command, another by way of indulgence.

"I once preached the gospel." What do I say, Paul says, did you not wrong me? Therefore you showed me great honor. For even while being flogged and persecuted (for he says this was a weakness of the flesh), I was proclaiming the gospel to you. And yet seeing me suffer these things, you neither were scandalized at me nor spat upon me. For you did not despise, he says, my trial in my flesh, a trial of good things again: the wounds, the imprisonments, the persecutions.
"But you know that because of weakness." That is, because of bodily weakness, namely, after bonds and blows and imprisonments, which I endured at the hands of those opposed to the preaching.
You know, he says, that in bodily weakness, that is, amid persecutions and dangers, I preached the gospel to you.

Secondly, he shows that he has reason to love them, when he says: "you know how, through infirmity of the flesh, I preached the gospel to you heretofore." Here he touches on three things that usually cause men to love one another. The first is the mutual help of fellowship, and this is also the cause of love being consolidated among men, according to Luke (22:28): "And you are they who have continued with me in my temptations; and I dispose to you as my Father hath disposed to me, a kingdom." Touching this he says: "And you know how, through infirmity of the flesh, I preached the gospel to you heretofore." Herein he does two things:

First, he recalls the tribulation he suffered among them;

Secondly, he shows how they stood by him (v. 13).

He says, therefore, with respect to the first: I say that "You have not injured me at all"; rather you have come to my aid. "For you know," i.e., are able to recall, "that I preached the gospel to you heretofore," i.e., in times past, "through infirmity of the flesh," i.e., with infirmity and affliction in my flesh, or with the many tribulations I suffered from the Jews who are of my flesh and persecuted me: "And I was with you in weakness and in fear and in much tribulation" (1 Cor 2:3); "Power is made perfect in infirmity" (2 Cor 12:9). And although this infirmity might have been reason for scorning me and a cause of temptation for you, according to Zacharias (13:7): "Strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered": nevertheless, "your temptation," which was "in my flesh," i.e., my tribulation, which was a source of temptation for you, "you despised not": "Despise not a man for his look" (Sir 11:2) because as the Lord says in Luke (10:16): "He that despiseth you, despiseth me." "Neither did you reject me" and my teaching, but you were willing to share my tribulations: "Woe to you that despisest, shall you not also be despised?" (Is 33:1).

The weakness in my body was no obstacle for you, but you received me as an angel of God, that is, as a messenger, a preacher sent from God (for that is an angel of God); and you received me like Christ Jesus, whom I was preaching to you. And so you truly received Christ Jesus, if you received me as an angel of God, in the same way you received Christ Jesus.

But you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. This he praises in them still more, that he was not disfigured in their eyes by his afflictions, but commended, since they knew that he suffered ruin for those who believe. So they received the Apostle as an angel of God, believing that what he preaches is the gift of God: thus deferring to him as though to the author himself, the Lord Jesus Christ.

And your temptation, which was in my flesh, you did not despise nor reject; but you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

An obscure passage, and one to be attended to more keenly. I, he says, long ago preached the Gospel to you as to little ones and sucklings, because of the weakness of your flesh, beginning from the lesser things and (so to speak) almost stammering among you. This dispensation and pretense of a weak preaching was indeed my management; but it was your temptation, to see whether those things would please you and seem great which in their own condition were lesser, and were brought forth by me as if lowly. And you, taking them not as small but as great, admired them so much that you welcomed me, who spoke them, as an angel and, to say more, as the Son of God. This temptation of yours, then, by which I was tempting you in the carnal proclamation of my discourse, was not despised, nor was it held cheap; but it had more dignity than I reckoned. This passage can also be explained thus: when I came to you, I did not come in the word of wisdom, but as a lowly and despised man, bringing nothing great: the Crucified. When, therefore, you saw me placed in a body subject to infirmities, promising the heavenly kingdoms, you did not laugh at me, nor did you reckon me worthy of contempt: for you understood that the lowliness of my flesh and the meanness of my very bearing came about for your temptation, namely, whether you would despise him who was thought pitiable by unbelievers; but on the contrary you welcomed that lowly, mean and despised man as an angel, and more than an angel. Or surely we can suspect that the Apostle, at the time when he first came to the Galatians, was sick; and that, though held back by some infirmity of his poor body, he nevertheless did not cease nor hold back his voice in silence from preaching the Gospel he had begun. For they relate that he often suffered a most severe pain of the head, and that this is the angel of Satan who was set upon him to buffet him in the flesh, lest he be lifted up. This infirmity and this sickness of the body was a temptation for those to whom the Gospel was proclaimed: whether they would despise him who promised sublime things, whom they saw subject to the sicknesses of the body. It can also be said that at the beginning of his coming to the Galatians he endured insults and persecutions and blows on his body from those who opposed the Gospel; and that this was the very greatest temptation for the Galatians, seeing the Apostle of Christ beaten. But when he says, as an angel, as Christ Jesus you welcomed me, he both shows that Christ is greater than an angel, Christ whom the Psalmist had sung as lesser according to the dispensation of the body, saying: "You have made him a little less than the angels" (Ps. 8:6); and he demonstrates that his own words at the beginning had such force that they were thought to be those of an angel and of Christ.

"Rather you received me as an angel of God." How then is it not unreasonable, he says, that one who is being persecuted and driven away should be received by you as an angel, and even as the Lord himself? Yet he is spat upon while he counsels and exhorts those things that lead to salvation.

And you, however, did not turn away from me; these trials of mine, that is, persecutions, wounds, and the like, did not lead you into temptation and did not cause you to despise and abhor me. And at the same time, in a subtle way, he also shames them, showing how much he endured for their sake from his opponents.

You so honored me, he says, as if I were more than a man. Is it not strange that at the time when I was being persecuted and driven out, you received me as an angel and as Christ, and were not offended, but now, when I counsel what is proper, you consider me an enemy and do not accept me?

The second thing that strengthens love among men is mutual love and affection toward one another, according to Proverbs (8:17): "I love them that love me." As to this he says: "but you received me as an angel of God," i.e., with the honor accorded to a messenger announcing God's words: "When you received of us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of men but (as it is indeed) the word of God" (1 Thes 2:13). For this reason preachers are called angels: "They shall seek the law at the priest's mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts" (Mal 2:7). And not only as an angel did you receive me, but "even as Christ Jesus," i.e., as though Christ Himself had come, Who, indeed, had come to them in him and spoke in him, according to 2 Corinthians (13:3): "Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me?" "He that receiveth you receiveth me" (Mt 10:40).

You were satisfied at the time when you received the gospel, because you were zealous at the outset. Yet now, since I do not see the finishing of the edifice, I am forced to say, "where is your satisfaction?"

What then was your blessedness? He says that they were held blessed among the other churches, because they were not broken by the Apostle's injuries, but grew in faith. For I bear you witness that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me. He shows that their devotion toward religion was so full that not only was he well received by them, but they were also found strong in faith: and, what goes further to their praise, they offered him almost all their goods to be spent. Hence he grieves the more, because so great a love had been overturned by perverse doctrine.

Here he shows perplexity and amazement, and desires to learn of themselves the reason of their change. Who, says he, hath deceived you, and caused a difference in your disposition towards me? Are ye not the same who attended and ministered to me, counting me more precious than your own eyes? what then has happened? whence this dislike? whence this suspicion? Is it because I have told you the truth? You ought on this very account to pay me increased honor and attention; instead of which "I am become your enemy, because I tell you the truth,"-for I can find no other reason but this. Observe too what humbleness of mind appears in his defence of himself; he proves not by his conduct to them, but by theirs to him that his language could not possibly have proceeded from unkind feeling. For he says not; How is it supposable that one, who has been scourged and driven about, and ill-treated a thousand things for your sakes, should now have schemes against you? But he argues from what they had reason to boast of, saying, How can one who has been honored by you, and received as an Angel, repay you by conduct the very opposite?

Where then is your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy, telling you the truth?

Blessed is he who walks in the way of the virtues, but only if he arrives all the way to the virtues. Nor does it profit to have withdrawn from vices unless you lay hold of the best things. For in good pursuits it is not so much the beginnings that are to be praised as the end. For just as in the vineyard there are many stages of the grape up to the press: first the vine must bud into leafy shoots and hold out hope in its blossoms; then, once the flower has fallen, the form of the future cluster is shaped, and little by little the grape, swelling, comes to its birth, so that, pressed in the winepresses, it may sweat out sweet must. So also in teaching there are single advances of blessedness: that someone hears the word of God, that he conceives it, that it grows in the womb of his soul and comes all the way to birth; that, when he has brought it forth, he nourishes it with milk and leads it through infancy, boyhood, adolescence and youth all the way to the perfect man. Since, then, the single stages, as we have said, have their blessedness according to their advances, if the end, and, so to speak, the finishing hand is lacking to the work, all the labor will become void; and it will be said: Where then is your blessedness? Although, he says, at the time when you received the Gospel according to the flesh I called you blessed because you were fervent in the beginnings, yet now, because I do not see the roof set upon the building, and the foundations hardly laid at all, I am compelled to say: Where then is your blessedness, for which, judging you blessed, I used to praise you before? For truly I myself also confess that you so loved me in the beginning, when I preached lowly things to you and was beset by persecutions, that, if it could have been done (and what he says is to be taken as hyperbole), you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me, so that I might see more with the lights of all of you. For you wished to be blind yourselves through an ineffable love toward me, so that the light of the Gospel might rise more fully in my heart; you wished my gain to grow by your losses: and this at that time when, whether because of the weakness of your flesh I announced small and lowly things to you as to little ones and sucklings, or because of the injuries of my own flesh, I did not seem worthy of belief.

— [PHOTIUS] "Who then was the blessing to you?" He was someone, not asked as a question, but as if marveling and lifting up their former faith and the blessing upon that faith. What it was, how great it was, wondrous, he says: from what great blessedness you have fallen. Or by interrogation, What was it? Remember, he says, how great your blessedness was: for I was blessing you very greatly; but now what? I reproach; therefore I am held in hatred. But why do I reproach? For your salvation. For if this were not so, how could I, without offering any other pretext of yours, the one who praises and blesses, have come to reproach?" [end of the excerpt by Photius] —

"the blessing to you." Who was, he says, the blessing to you, whom I and many others blessed you for, concerning obedience and submission to the Gospel? Who then was he? he says; for now I do not see him. Where, he says, are the zealously accomplished works of faith? for he has put the who instead of where.

"your eyes." I know, Paul says, that you regard me as more precious than your own eyes because of my long-standing preaching.

In bewilderment and amazement he says: what has become of your former blessedness? That is, where has all that gone for which everyone called you blessed, as those devoted to your teacher? What is it now? What has your former blessedness turned into? Now I do not see it, since you are hostile toward me.

Previously, on account of my preaching, you considered me dearer even than your own eyes; so what has happened now that you suspect me as an enemy? For it would be strange if the one whom you so honored were to say these things to you with hostile intent.

But he then rebukes them for their change of heart; hence he says, "Where is then your blessedness?" As if to say: Did not men think you blessed for honoring me and accepting my preaching? "Where is thy fear, thy fortitude, thy patience and the perfection of thy ways?" (Job 4:6).

The third thing that strengthens love is doing good to one another. As to this he says: "For I bear you witness that, if it could be done," i.e., had been just to do so (for that can be done which it is just to do) or had been to the advantage of the Church, "you would have plucked out your own eyes and would have given them to me." As if to say: You loved me so much that you would have given me not only your external goods but your very eyes.

Wherefore the apostle himself also in every case uses stringent language to the Churches, after the Lord's example; and conscious of his own boldness, and of the weakness of his hearers, he says to the Galatians: "Am I your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" Thus also people in health do not require a physician, do not require him as long as they are strong; but those who are ill need his skill. Thus also we who in our lives are ill of shameful lusts and reprehensible excesses, and other inflammatory effects of the passions, need the Saviour. And He administers not only mild, but also stringent medicines. The bitter roots of fear then arrest the eating sores of our sins. Wherefore also fear is salutary, if bitter.

Therefore, dearest brother, endeavour that the undisciplined should not be consumed and perish, that as much as you can, by your salutary counsels, you should rule the brotherhood, and take counsel of each one with a view to his salvation. Strait and narrow is the way through which we enter into life, but excellent and great is the reward when we enter into glory. Let those who have once made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven please God in all things, and not offend God's priests nor the Lord's Church by the scandal of their wickedness. And if, for the present, certain of our brethren seem to be made sorry by us, let us nevertheless remain in our wholesome persuasion, knowing that an apostle also has said, "Am I therefore become your enemy because I tell you the truth? " But if they shall obey us, we have gained our brethren, and have formed them as well to salvation as to dignity by our address. But if some of the perverse persons refuse to obey, let us follow the same apostle, who says, "If I please men, I should not be the servant of Christ." If we cannot please some, so as to make them please Christ, let us assuredly, as far as we can, please Christ our Lord and God, by observing His precepts.

Have I then become your enemy, telling you the truth? He says this because it cannot be, he says, that I should be an enemy to you, from whom I have experienced such great kindnesses. But because no one wishes to be reproved when he errs, therefore I seem an enemy to you, since I justly reprove you.

But now, because I have begun to call you on from the elements and syllables and the reading of boys to greater studies, so that you may hold books in your hands and may learn words full of learning and of meanings, you kick back, you are angry, the perfection of teachings seems burdensome to you; and you are changed to other feelings to such a degree that me, whom you had received as an angel and as Christ, to whom you wished to hand over your eyes, you now hold as an enemy, because I announce to you the full truth. And he has elegantly ended the sentence, saying: Have I then become your enemy, telling you the truth? in order to show that the beginnings of the preaching were not so much the truth as the shadow and image of the truth. Like this is that famous sentence of the poet among the Romans (Terence, Andria 1.1): Compliance begets friends, truth hatred. But see how much better the one here is than that one; for the Apostle tempered this sentence for those whom he had called foolish, whom he had named little ones, and made it particular, since he directed it properly to the persons and to the Galatians. But that one, declaring it both general and as holding so among all men, erred badly. For compliance, by which he thought friends are made, once truth is taken away, is not so much compliance as flattery and fawning; and it is plain that these ought to be called hidden enmities rather than friendships. At the same time this too must be considered, that today also, so long as we explain the Scriptures according to the letter to little ones and sucklings, and to those in whose hearts Christ never grows up nor advances in age and wisdom and grace with God and men, we are praised, looked up to, held in admiration. But when we have begun a little to call them on to pass over to greater things, from being our heralds they become enemies, and they would rather follow the Jews than the apostles, who, withdrawing from the teaching and traditions of the Pharisees, entered into Christ himself, the propitiatory, and the perfection of the Law; nor do they deign to accept the divine word, which bids the teachers of the Church to climb to loftier doctrines, to raise the voice with all their strength, and not to fear the clamor of the little ones barking around them, saying: "Go up on a lofty mountain, you who bring good tidings to Sion. Lift up your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. Lift it up, do not fear" (Isa. 40:9).

"So I have become your enemy." Elsewhere, he says, I do not know any cause for enmity other than that I deliver to you truths and teachings that lead to salvation, by which it would even have been fitting for you to increase your love toward me.

I know of no other reason for the enmity, he says, except that I told you the truth and exposed those who were in error regarding the dogmas. But for this you ought rather to love me even more, as one who has fulfilled the duty of a guardian.

Then when he says: "Am I then become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?", he states the cause of a supposed hatred.

First, the cause on the part of the Apostle;

Secondly, on the part of the false brethren (v. 17).

He says therefore: If you have done me so much good, are you to believe that "I am become your enemy because I tell you the truth?" The word "enemy" used here can be interpreted in two ways: in one way as meaning that he hates them; in this case the interpretation is "have I become your enemy," i.e., hate you? Hence what follows, namely, "because I tell you the truth," can be taken as an indication of hatred, even though telling the truth at the proper time and place is a sign of love. In another way, the word "enemy" can be taken in a passive sense, i.e., so that he is hated by them; then "have I become your enemy" is interpreted as "Do you hate me?" and this because I tell you the truth, so that telling the truth is set down as the cause of hatred. For men who tell the truth are hated by evil men, since the truth engenders hatred: "They have hated him that rebuketh in the gate: and I have abhorred him that speaketh perfectly" (Am 5:10).

But on the other hand, it is said in Proverbs (28:23): "He that rebuketh a man shall afterward find favor with him more than he that by a flattering tongue deceiveth him." I answer that the solution to this can be gathered from what is said in Proverbs (9:9): "Rebuke not a scorner, lest he hate thee. Rebuke a wise man and he will love thee." For if the one corrected loves the corrector, it is a sign of virtue; conversely, it is a sign of malice, if he should hate him. For since a man naturally hates what is contrary to what he loves, then if you hate one who corrects you for evil, it is obvious that you love the evil; but if you love him, you indicate that you hate sin. For at first, when men are corrected, they are attached to their sins—that is why a sinner's first reaction is to hate the one correcting him; but after the correction he puts aside his attachment to sin and loves the one correcting him. And therefore the passage from Proverbs expressly says that later he will find favor with him.

Since emulate signifies two things—one when someone emulates what he finds pleasing because it is good and another when people are emulators because they feel envy—these people, he says, emulate you in a bad way, by which he means that they are imitators through envy.… When he adds the phrase "so that you may emulate them" [meaning] "that you may follow them," he has thus used the double sense of emulation in different places, since emulation is imitation, and especially when it is also directed to what is good.… [He continues: ] "Emulate therefore better gifts—not those of Jewish law, which are not gifts and are not better; but emulate those things which are good and better gifts. That is, whatever belongs to faith and love, emulate that with regard to Christ and follow it. It is always good to emulate better things. Emulation as such is not good, but the emulation of better things is always good, and not only when I am present."

They emulate you not well: but they wish to shut you out, so that you may emulate them. He signifies that they were overturned by the envy of the Jews; for, seeing them advance so in the Gospel and have such great love for the Apostle, these contrived to deceive them. For they were enemies to the apostles because of the Law, so that, while the name of the Savior remained, they might make them Jews, rejoicing in their overthrow; for they could not bear to hear that the grace promised to themselves had been given to the uncircumcised Gentiles. Therefore they wished them to become their imitators, so that they might be circumcised after their manner.

It is a wholesome emulation which leads to an imitation of virtue, but an evil one, which seduces from virtue him who is in the right path. And this is the object of those persons, who would deprive you of perfect knowledge, and impart to you that which is mutilated and spurious, and this for no other purpose than that they may occupy the rank of teachers, and degrade you, who now stand higher than themselves, to the position of disciples. For this is the meaning of the words "that ye may seek them." But I, says he, desire the reverse, that ye may become a model for them, and a pattern of a higher perfection: a thing which actually happened when I was present with you...

They emulate you not well: but they wish to shut you out, that you may emulate them. But emulate the good in a good thing always: and not only when I am present with you.

They emulate well who, when they see graces, gifts and powers in certain people, themselves desire to be such: and they strive to imitate the faith, life and diligence of those people, through which they merited those things, so that they too may be able to attain the things that are good and worthy of emulation. Of these the Apostle also says: "Emulate spiritual things: but rather that you may prophesy". And next: "So you also, since you are emulators of spiritual things, seek to abound for the edification of the Church". And again: "Therefore, brothers, emulate to prophesy, and do not forbid to speak in tongues". But they emulate not well who do not so much desire to be better themselves, by imitating those who are worthy of emulation, as wish to make those very people worse, and to drag them backward by a perverse emulation. Let it be said by way of example: someone is a Christian; he reads Moses and the prophets; he knows that all things went before for that people in shadow and in image, but were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come down. He understands circumcision not so much of the foreskin as of the ears and of the heart. He has risen with Christ: he seeks the things that are above. He has been freed from the burden and slavery of the Law, which commands: touch not, taste not, defile not. If anyone should wish to persuade this man by the words of the Scriptures to receive the things that are written not through tropology but according to the killing letter, so that he becomes a Jew outwardly, not inwardly, that person emulates him not well: rather he hastens to drag back one who is advancing at a swift pace toward greater things, so that the other may instead emulate him who is going backward; or at the least he keeps him from advancing much further. He speaks, therefore, to the Galatians, who had been induced by the champions of the Law to imitate them, when those men ought rather to have imitated the Galatians.

This is said of that zeal and perverse emulation of which it is also said elsewhere: "Do not emulate among the evildoers" (Ps. 36:1); and here: They emulate you not well. But we find also another zeal, with which the sons of Jacob were zealous against their brother Joseph (Gen. 37 ff.), and Miriam and Aaron against Moses, the friend of the Lord (Num. 12). For neither the former nor the latter were stirred to zeal in order to become better than Joseph and Moses, but because they grieved that those men were better. This zeal is a near neighbor of envy. It would be a long task if I wished to bring forth from the treasury of the Scriptures all the kinds of zeal, whether good or bad. We read of the good zeal of Phinehas (Num. 25), of Elijah (1 Kings 19), of Mattathias (1 Macc. 2), and of the apostle Judas (but not the traitor), who on account of the remarkable power of zeal in him received also the name of Zealot (Acts 1). And bad zeal, as that of Cain against Abel (Gen. 4), and of others against others. And the zeal of a husband, of which it is written: "And the spirit of zeal come upon him" (Num. 5). Unless perhaps this zeal is intermediate, and can be taken neither in a good nor in a bad sense, but, standing between the two, is rather called jealousy. Otherwise: those who were of the circumcision, seeing that the Galatians from the Gentiles abounded in the powers of the Holy Spirit, while they themselves did not speak in tongues, did not have gifts of healings, nor the grace of prophecy, were spurred on by the goads of zeal and desired to bring them over to the burdens of the Law, so that they too might begin to become like them.

He says this with reference to those evil teachers. "For seeing your conspicuous faith," he says, "they are grieved and all try by every means to rob you of those goods and subject you to their own authority." For that is what he means by writing "that you may emulate them."

— [OECUMENIUS] "They envy you." He says they do not welcome the same faith in Christ for your benefit, but in order to exclude you from it and persuade themselves to follow, because such a plan has been formulated against your deception. [end of the excerpt by Oecumenius] —

"not rightly." For there is also good envy, when someone so envies that he imitates virtue. And there is also bad envy, when someone envies in such a way as to drive the virtuous person out of virtue.

"but they desire to exclude you." Paul says, They wish to shut you off and to carry you away from the true knowledge, so that having become your teachers themselves, they may lead you to the same envy and imitation. For this reason they carry you away from true knowledge and bring you to the law.

Zeal is a praiseworthy thing when someone imitates the virtue of another, but it becomes bad when someone strives to remove the virtuous person from perfection. And these people are trying to exclude you, that is, to deprive you of the more perfect state and knowledge in Christ and to cast you into the less perfect, which consists in the law, so that you would regard them as teachers, be zealous for and imitate them as disciples. But I wished that you would be guides to perfection both for them and for all. And so it was when I was with you. He points to this very same thing below as well.

Then when he says, "They are zealous in your regard not well," he states another supposed cause, namely, on the part of the false brethren.

First, he states it;

Secondly, he refutes it (v. 18).

As to the first it should be noted that, as has been said above, certain false brethren, converted from Judaism, went about the churches of the Gentiles, preaching the observance of the Law. Because Paul opposed them, they slandered him. They did this not so much with an eye to their salvation as to get rid of Paul. Hence the Apostle says, "They are zealous in your regard," i.e., they do not allow you (whom they love with a love not of friendship but of self-interest) to associate with us. For jealous rivalry is zeal that arises from any love whatsoever and does not brook what is loved to be shared. But because their love for them was not good: first of all, because they did not love them so as to advantage them but for their own gain—and this is obvious from the fact that they wanted to keep the Apostle away from them as one opposed to their own advantage—and secondly, because this was a source of harm to the Gentiles—for they sought from them an advantage by which the latter would suffer harm; for these reasons he says, "They are zealous in your regard but not well," because they are not interested in your welfare. And this is obvious, because "they would exclude you that you might be zealous for them," i.e., that you might admit none but them: "Envy not the unjust man and do not follow his ways" (Prov 3:31); "Let not thy heart envy sinners" (Prov 23:17).

But emulate the better gifts, emulate the good always, and not only when I am present with you. The better gifts are the spiritual ones; having imitated these, they will have effect before God. These are the spiritual goods which he wishes them always to imitate, not for a time, as before, or only while he is present, only afterward to turn to something else; but he wishes them to persevere in the good from now on.

Here he hints that his absence had been the cause of this, and that the true blessing was for disciples to hold right opinions not only in the presence but also in the absence of their master. But as they had not arrived at this point of perfection, he makes every effort to place them there.

And since it is natural that the greater should be made from the lesser, not the lesser from the greater, he also says: Emulate the good in a good thing, that is, do not imitate the champions of Jewish observance, but imitate the things that are good. For just as one who imitates someone's riches, power and rank emulates not so much good things as things that ought to be shunned, so you, on the contrary, emulate the good in a good thing, seeking spiritual things rather than carnal ones, so that it is not they who teach you to be Jews, but you who teach them to be Christians. And do this always, so that with persevering step you may be able to reach the end of the good work. For indeed you emulated the good in a good thing formerly, when I was with you; but after I departed from you, you lost everything I had handed on to you, drawn away from a sure anchorage and a trusty harbor out again into the deep by the ebbing wave. Nor is it any wonder if, when the Apostle departed, the vessel of election, in whom Christ the Lord spoke, the Galatians were changed, since even now we see the very same thing happen in the churches too. For if ever there happens to be in a church a teacher adorned in speech and in life, who rouses his hearers to virtues as if with certain goads, we see the whole people hasten, burn with fervor and run to and fro over almsgiving, fasting, chastity, the receiving of the poor, the burial of the dead and other such things. But when he has departed, we see it little by little wither away, and, its food withdrawn, grow thin, turn pale and languish, and the ruin follow of everything that had flourished before. Wherefore, since the harvest is great but the laborers are few (Matt. 9:37), let us pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers to reap, who may reap and gather the ears of the Christian people that stand in the Church, made ready to be the wheat to come, and, carrying them into the barns, may by no means allow them to perish.

He wishes to show that those who now are overturning them, and persuading them to observe to the law, and by this preparing them to become zealous imitators of it, had long ago envied them in the knowledge of the Gospel, when Paul was present and was teaching them.

"It is good, however," he says, "to strive enthusiastically in what is good always, and not only when I am present with you." And he shows that they have been deceived during his absence.

Do you not see, he hints at the fact that they rivaled everyone in perfection when Paul was among them? And he also gives to understand that his absence gave rise to this evil. It would be excellent, he therefore says, if not only in the presence of the teacher, but also in his absence, the disciples thought what was proper.

But he rejects this when he says, "But be zealous for that which is good in a good thing always." As if to say: You ought not to be zealous for them in their teaching; but be zealous for a good teacher, i.e., for me and those like me: "And who is he that can hurt you if you be zealous of the good?" (1 Pet. 3:13). But because there can be evil in a good teacher, he adds, "be zealous of the good" teacher, yet say "in a good thing," i.e., in that which is good: "Follow after charity and be zealous for spiritual goods" (1 Cor 14:1).

Now, although the Apostle speaks of himself, according to a Gloss, when he says, "be zealous of the good," yet he adds "in a good thing," because as he says: "I am not conscious of any thing, yet I am not hereby justified" (1 Cor 4:4). But because some are zealous for a good teacher in his presence alone, he adds: "always, and not only when I am present with you"; because zeal for the good, if it continues even when the teacher is absent, is an indication that it proceeds from love and fear of God Who sees all: "Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not serving to the eye, as pleasing men, but in simplicity of heart, fearing God" (Col 3:22).

"Little children," says our teacher, "a little while longer I am with you." That is why Paul also instructs the Galatians in these words: "My little children, with whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you." And again he writes to the Corinthians: "For though you may have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet you have not many fathers. For in Christ I have begotten you through the gospel." On this account "a eunuch shall not enter into God's assembly," that is, the man who is unproductive and unfruitful both in conduct and in word; but blessed are those who have made themselves eunuchs, free from all sin, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven by their abstinence from the world.

"For," says he, "I have begotten you through the gospel; " and "Ye are my children, of whom I travail again in birth." Now was absolutely fulfilled that promise of the Spirit which was given by the word of Joel: "In the last days will I pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and their daughters shall prophesy; and upon my servants and upon my handmaids will I pour out of my Spirit.

But so did circumstances require him to "become all things to all, in order to gain all; " "travailing in birth with them until Christ should be formed in them; " and "cherishing, as it were a nurse," the little ones of faith, by teaching them some things "by way of indulgence, not by way of command"-for it is one thing to indulge, another to bid-permitting a temporary licence of re-marriage on account of the "weakness of the flesh," just as Moses of divorcing on account of "the hardness of the heart.

That there are also some souls that conceive offspring, the prophet made clear when he said: "from fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and travailed and gave birth to a spirit of salvation which you made upon the earth". For just as in those who are pregnant the seed is formed and shaped, so also in the soul that receives the word, the conception of the word is gradually formed and shaped within it. And this I think is what Paul says to the Galatians: "my children, whom I again bring forth in travail until Christ be formed in you", which is as though he were to say: until the word be formed and made manifest in you. In the epistle to Timothy he says likewise that a woman shall be saved "through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". But who is this woman, if not the soul that conceives the word of God and of truth, and gives birth to good works like to Christ? But it is irrational to suppose that what he says was said of a bodily bearing: "the woman, being seduced, fell into transgression; but she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". Therefore the souls that have newly received the word and, being still established as pregnant, have not yet borne fruit in it, having it intelligibly in the womb, cannot endure the discourse that stands "in the holy place" opposing the truth, nor stand firm so as not to be seduced by its persuasions.

And by "sight" we mean the sight of the Word and of wisdom and of truth and of righteousness and of peace and of everything whatsoever that is the only-begotten of God. And you will understand the sight of the Word and the sight of wisdom when you have understood what the Apostle says: "my children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you". For understanding Christ formed in someone, you will consequently, according to a formation of this kind, see also the sight of Christ.

The pregnant woman is said to be the soul which has recently conceived the word of God. Now concerning such a conception we read it written also in another place: "from fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb, and we have given birth." Those, therefore, who conceive and immediately give birth—these are to be reckoned not as women, but as men, and perfect men. Hear, finally, also the prophet saying: "if the earth has given birth in one day, and a nation has been born at once." This is the generation of the perfect, which is born immediately, on the same day, as soon as it has been conceived. But lest it seem new to you that we have said men give birth, we have already long since set forth how you ought to take the names of the members, that you may withdraw from bodily senses and grasp the understanding of the inner man. But if you wish that I satisfy you still further in this also from the Scriptures, hear the Apostle saying: "my little children, whom I again bring forth in travail, until Christ be formed in you." Perfect, therefore, and strong men are those who immediately, as soon as they conceive, give birth—that is, those who bring the conceived word of faith forth into works. But the soul which conceives and retains in the womb and does not give birth, this one is called a woman, just as the prophet also says: "the pains of childbirth have come upon her, and the power of giving birth is not in her." This soul, then, which now on account of its weakness is called a woman, when two men are quarreling with one another and in the contest bringing forth stumbling-blocks—which the contention of words is always wont to have—is struck and scandalized, so that it casts out and loses the word of faith which it had faintly conceived; and this is the quarrel and contention "unto the subversion of the hearers." If, therefore, the soul which has been scandalized casts out the word not yet formed, he who scandalized it is said to suffer loss. Do you wish to know that in some the word is formed, in some not yet formed? The word of the Apostle plainly teaches us, which we recalled above, when he says: "until Christ be formed in you"; but Christ is the Word of God. By this he shows that at the time when he was writing, the Word of God was not yet formed in them; if, therefore, it comes forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss.

Let teachers therefore hear, lest perhaps they entrust the words of God to a "defiled" soul, to a "harlot" soul, to an unfaithful soul, lest perhaps they cast "what is holy to the dogs and pearls before swine", but let them choose clean souls, "virgins" "in the simplicity of the faith which is in Christ", let them commit to them the secret mysteries, let them speak forth to them the word of God and the hidden things of faith, that in them "Christ may be formed" through faith. Or do you not know that from this seed of the word of God which is sown, Christ is born in the heart of the hearers? For the Apostle too says this: "until Christ be formed in us". The soul therefore conceives from this seed of the word and forms the conceived word within itself, until it brings forth the spirit of the fear of God.

For he says, "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you; ".
Receive the features, and the image, and the manliness of Christ, the likeness of the form of the Word being stamped upon them, and begotten in them by a true knowledge and faith, so that in each one Christ is spiritually born. And, therefore, the Church swells and travails in birth until Christ is formed in us,

Sons are spoken of in many senses, sometimes as by love, sometimes as by nature, sometimes as by blood, sometimes even as by religion. This is what Paul means now by "my sons," either because when the new birth occurs through faithful baptism, he who guides the baptized toward maturity or receives them when fully ready is called their father, or because when he calls them back into Christ he makes them his own sons.

My little children, of whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you. At first he had begotten them through faith in baptism; but because, born as if by a miscarriage, they were found deformed and weak, he now, with the pain of counsel, re-forms them into Christ. For, conceiving faith but paying no heed to the meaning of faith, they are said not to have Christ formed in their souls; for if they had understood the grace of God in Christ, they would not have been carried over into Judaism after faith.

Observe his perplexity and perturbation, "Brethren, I beseech you:" "My little children, of whom I am again in travail:" He resembles a mother trembling for her children. "Until Christ be formed in you." Behold his paternal tenderness, behold this despondency worthy of an Apostle. Observe what a wail he utters, far more piercing than of a woman in travail;-Ye have defaced the likeness, ye have destroyed the kinship, ye have changed the form, ye need another regeneration and refashioning; nevertheless I call you children, abortions and monsters though ye be. However, he does not express himself in this way, but spares them, unwilling to strike, and to inflict wound upon wound. Wise physicians do not cure those who have fallen into a long sickness all at once, but little by little, lest they should faint and die. And so is it with this blessed man; for these pangs were more severe in proportion as the force of his affection was stronger. And the offense was of no trivial kind. And as I have ever said and ever will say, even a slight fault mars the appearance and distorts the figure of the whole.

My little children, of whom I travail again, until Christ be formed in you.

With what great difficulties and pain offspring are brought forth from the womb, the first curse declares, saying: "In sorrow you shall bear children" (Gen. 3:16). Wishing therefore to show the solicitude of teachers for their disciples, and what feelings they suffer lest their followers fall away from salvation, Paul says: My little children, of whom I travail again. For he who in another place had said as a father: "Though you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, yet not many fathers" (1 Cor. 4:15), now speaks in Christ no longer as a father but as a mother, so that they may recognize in him the anxiety and the tender devotion of both parents. Something of the sort Moses too said of the people: "Did I receive all this people in my womb" (Num. 11:12)? Which of us, do you think, is so anxious for the salvation of his disciples that he is tormented not for a few hours, or at most for two or three days, but for the whole time of his life, until Christ is formed in them? The example he has taken of a pregnant woman, conceiving and forming the seed within herself, must be carefully held to, so that we may understand what is said. Nature is not to be blushed at, but revered. For just as the seed is first cast without form into a woman's womb, so that it clings to its furrows and floor as if with a kind of glue (and the prophet too, remembering his own beginning, says of it: "Your eyes saw my unformed state" (Ps. 138:16)); then through nine months, the blood being held back, the future man is curdled, given a body, nourished and articulated into parts; so that, after it has stirred in the womb, at the appointed time it is poured forth into the light, and is born with as great difficulties as those with which it is afterwards nursed lest it perish: so too the seed of the word of Christ, when it has fallen into the soul of the hearer, grows by its own stages, and, to pass over many things (for we can easily transfer the bodily description to the spiritual understanding), it remains in a precarious state for as long as it takes until he who conceived gives birth. Nor is the end of the effort reached at once in having brought forth; rather, then comes the beginning of another labor: to lead the suckling infancy, with diligent nourishment and pains, up to the full age of Christ. And just as in marriage the husband's seed is often the cause that children are not begotten, sometimes a barren wife does not retain the seed, frequently neither is fit for begetting, and on the contrary both are fruitful: so too among those who sow the word of God this fourfold division holds: either the teacher indeed fulfills his office, but the hearer is barren; or the hearer is of good disposition, but through the teacher's want of skill the seed of the word perishes; or surely the one who is taught is as senseless as the one who instructs; and rarely does it happen that master and disciple are in accord with each other, namely that the one teaches as much as the other can draw in, or that the one taught takes in as much as the teacher pours in. But now we are all judges. We do not know what number a psalm is, what part of prophecy, what chapter of the Law, and by mere facility of speech we boldly interpret what we in no way understand. It is no concern of ours that Christ be formed in the people, that each one, returning to his own home, may have the seed of the word of God, so that when he has conceived it he may say with the prophet: "From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth; we have made children of your salvation upon the earth" (Isa. 26:17, 18). Such people pass over into the apostles, and deserve to hear from the Savior: "Whoever shall do the will of my Father, he is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Matt. 12:50): the diversity of their progress being shown in the different names. Christ is also formed in the heart of believers when all mysteries are laid open to them, and the things that seemed obscure become clear. But this too must be observed: that he who through sin had in a certain manner ceased to be a man is conceived by the master through penitence, and the forming of Christ in him is promised once again. This is against the Novatians, who will not have those whom sins have once crushed formed anew.

Let us give an example, so that what is commanded to the daughter of Zion, when it is said: Be in pain, and act manfully, like a woman giving birth, we may refer not to her punishment but to her benefit. Paul says to the Galatians: My little children, with whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you. And he was in pain so long, and in labor so long, until he begot again through repentance those who had perished through sin.

Humans are conceived in their mother's womb in order to be formed, yet only when fully formed do they go into labor. One might be surprised by his statement: "You with whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you." We are to understand this travail to stand for the agonies of concern that they might be born in Christ. Then he labors for them once again because of the dangers of their seduction, by which he sees them being disturbed.

Perchance therefore sinners have been alienated from a certain womb, wherein that charity was suffering pains, which speaketh through the Apostle, “Of whom again I am in labour, until Christ be formed in you.” Expect thou therefore; be formed: do not to thyself ascribe a judgment which perchance thou knowest not. Carnal thou art as yet, conceived thou hast been: from that very time when thou hast received the name of Christ, by a sort of sacrament thou hast been born in the bowels of a mother. For not only out of bowels a man is born, but also in bowels. First he is born in bowels, in order that he may be able to be born of bowels. Wherefore it hath been said even to Mary, “For that which is born in thee, is of the Holy Spirit.” Not yet of Her It had been born, but already in Her It had been born. Therefore there are born within the bowels of the Church certain little ones, and a good thing it is that being formed they should go forth, so that they drop not by miscarriage. Let the mother bear thee, not miscarry. If patient thou shalt have been, even until thou be formed, even until in thee there be the sure doctrine of truth, the maternal bowels ought to keep thee. But if by thy impatience thou shalt have shaken the sides of thy mother, with pain indeed she expelleth thee out, but more to thy loss than to hers.
Christ is "formed in you" by nothing else but irreproachable faith and the way of gospel.

"My little children." Even if, Paul says, you have corrupted the form of Christ and the image upon you, yet you are still my little children. And he says "little children," those small and unbegotten, or aborted infants, and lacking birth. For this reason he did not say "children," but "my little children."

"until Christ be formed in you." You have corrupted, he says, the image of Christ in you, which you wore through baptism. As many as were baptized into Christ, you have clothed yourselves with Christ, and you have lost his form, and his being as members. There is therefore need of another birth, which will again imprint upon you the divine form of Christ. What then? Again I labor you by teaching. Again I beget, through catechesis, until you are again imprinted with the divine form of Christ. What then do the Novatians say in response to these things? For behold, I write these things plainly to the faithful.

— [CYRIL] Those whom I labor, until the great and excellent characters of the divinity of Christ be formed into your minds. [end of the excerpt from Cyril of Alexandria] —

He imitates a mother trembling for her children. You, he says, have distorted the image of Christ which you had within you from baptism, and you require a new rebirth and re-creation, so that the image of Christ may again appear in you and His character be imprinted upon you. Again I am in the pangs of birth, again I am regenerating you through teaching. But I do not despair. Therefore I also call you children, so that you too would not lose hope. And this is against the Novatians: Paul regenerates and renews the Galatians, but they (the Novatians) do not accept correction through repentance.

Above, the Apostle dismissed the false cause of his correcting the Galatians; here he discloses the true cause, which is sorrow for their imperfection.

First, he expresses the heartfelt sorrow of which he spoke;

Secondly, a desire to manifest this sorrow (v. 20);

Thirdly, he gives the cause of the sorrow (v. 20): "because I am ashamed for you."

This sorrow proceeded from charity, because he grieved for their sins: "I beheld the transgressors and I pined away; because they kept not thy word" (Ps 118:158). And so he addresses them in words of charity, saying, "My little children." He purposely does not call them sons, but little children, to indicate the imperfection whereby they had become small: "As unto little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not meat" (1 Cor 3:1).

It should be noted that during parturition a child is called a little one. And this is what they were, because they needed to be born again, even though parents according to the flesh bring forth their child only once. Accordingly he says to them, "of whom I am in labor again." For he was in labor of them during their first conversion; but since they had now turned from the one who called them, to another gospel, they needed to be brought forth anew. Hence he says, "I am in labor," i.e., with labor and pain I bring them forth into the light of faith. In these words the Apostle bares his grief. Hence a man's conversion is called a birth: "They bow themselves to bring forth young" (Job 39:3); "And being with child she cried, travailing in birth and was in pain to be delivered" (Rev 12:2). Therefore it is because of his pain that he rebukes them so sharply, as a woman cries aloud because of the pains of childbirth: "I will speak now as a woman in labor" (Is 42:14).

The reason for the iterated travail is that you are not perfectly formed. Hence he says: "until Christ be formed in you," i.e., until you receive His likeness, which you have lost through your sin. He does not say, "That you may be formed in Christ," but "until Christ be formed in you," to make it resound more terrifyingly on their ears. For Christ is formed in the heart by "formed faith": "That Christ might dwell in your hearts by faith" (Eph 3:17). But when one does not have "formed faith," Christ has already died in him: "Until the day dawn and the day star arise in your hearts" (2 Pet. 1:19). Thus Christ grows in a man according to his progress in the faith; conversely, as it diminishes, He recedes. Therefore, when the faith of a man is rendered "unformed" by sin, Christ is not formed in him; and so, because there was not a formed faith in them, they needed to be brought forth in the womb again until Christ be formed in them through faith, i.e., "formed faith," which works through love. Or, "until Christ be formed in you," i.e., through you Christ appear finely formed to others.

The real Son of God is at your side. He is beginning to turn you into the same kind of thing as Himself. He is beginning, so to speak, to 'inject' His kind of life and thought, His Zoe, into you; beginning to turn the tin soldier into a live man. The part of you that does not like it is the part that is still tin.
Mere Christianity, Book 4, Chapter 7: Let's Pretend

But I would wish to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I am confounded in you. He wishes to rebuke them in person, so as to change his voice from praise of them to censure, so that they might be confounded in a twofold way, both by their own error and by the shame of the Apostle, which he suffered before those to whom he had preferred them.

Observe his warmth, his inability to refrain himself, and to conceal these his feelings; such is the nature of love; nor is he satisfied with words, but desires to be present with them, and so, as he says, to change his voice, that is, to change to lamentation, to shed tears, to turn every thing into mourning. For he could not by letter show his tears or cries of grief, and therefore he ardently desires to be present with them.

I know not, says he, what to say, or what to think. How is it, that ye who by dangers, which ye endured for the faith's sake, and by miracles, which ye performed through faith, had ascended to the highest heaven, should suddenly be brought to such a depth of degradation as to be drawn aside to circumcision or sabbaths, and should rely wholly upon Judaizers? Hence in the beginning he says, "I marvel that ye are so quickly removing," and here, "I am perplexed about you," as if he said, What am I to speak? What am I to utter? What am I to think? I am bitterly perplexed. And so he must needs weep, as the prophets do when in perplexity; for not only admonition but mourning also is a form in which solicitous attention is often manifested. And what he said in his speech to those at Miletus, "By the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one with tears, he says here also, "and to change my voice." (Acts 20:31.) When we find ourselves overcome by perplexity and helplessness which come contrary to expectation, we are driven to tears; and so Paul admonished them sharply, and endeavored to shame them, then in turn soothed them, and lastly he wept. And this weeping is not only a reproof but a blandishment; it does not exasperate like reproof, nor relax like indulgent treatment, but is a mixed remedy, and of great efficacy in the way of exhortation. Having thus softened and powerfully engaged their hearts by his tears, he again advances to the contest, and lays down a larger proposition, proving that the Law itself was opposed to its being kept. Before, he produced the example of Abraham, but now (what is more cogent) he brings forward the Law itself enjoining them not to keep itself, but to leave off. So that, says he, you must abandon the Law, if you would obey it, for this is its own wish: this however he does not say expressly, but enforces it in another mode, mixing up with it an account of facts.

But I would wish to be with you now, and to change my voice, because I am confounded in you.

Divine Scripture edifies even when it is read; but it profits much more if it is turned from letters into voice, so that he who had taught through the Epistle may, being present, instruct his hearers. For the living voice has great force: a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, which is uttered and articulated with the very delivery with which it was generated in its own man's heart. The Apostle, therefore, knowing that speech addressed to those who are present has greater force, desires to change the epistolary voice, the voice confined in letters, into presence: and, because this was more expedient for those who had been perverted in error, to draw them back to the truth by living speech. And this for the reason that he was confounded in them: which indeed is said more properly in Greek. For Ἀποροῦμαι signifies not so much confusion, which among them is called αἰσχύνη or σύγχυσις, as need and want. This, then, is the sense: I would wish to be with you now, and to utter in person, being present myself, the voice of my letters, because I am in need in you. For I do not have the fruits that teachers are accustomed to have from their disciples; and the seed of teachings has been sown in vain, since I suffer utter destitution in you: so that I could break out in the words of Jeremiah: "I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me" (Jer. 15:10). This passage can also be interpreted another way: Paul the apostle, who had become a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews (1 Cor. 9), and to those who were under the Law as though he himself were under the Law, and weak to the weak, that he might gain the weak: according to the character of those whom he desired to save, he would change his voice, and, in the manner of actors (for indeed he was made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men [1 Cor. 4]), he would turn his bearing and his voices into various shapes. Not that he was what he pretended to be; but that he only seemed to be what was of profit to the others. He perceives that the Galatians need another teaching, that they must be saved by another way, not by that by which they had first been brought over from heathenism to the faith of Christ: and he is compelled to say: I would wish now to be with you, and to change my voice, because I am confounded in you. I do not see, he says, that I am of profit if I speak the things that I spoke before; because of which, not knowing what to do, and drawn in different directions, I am torn, confounded and rent apart.
